The game advertises itself as a Big Brother simulator, but it doesn't [i]quite[/i] reach that level of depth and intrigue that kind of premise could reach.

However, I don't think Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You isn't a bad game at all. I think it's definitely a concept that is executed well. You play as an investigator who's collecting information on a variety of people through public channels, such as social media outlets, and private channels such as one's email. These pieces of information are used as evidence to solve the crime you're assigned to.

There is some decision-making in the game and it was interesting to see how the conversation changes between characters after performing certain actions. There are a couple of routes to take, but ultimately, the resolution is relatively the same. I don't mind this that much, and I honestly think true choice games are difficult to make, unless you have the resources as a studio.

However, the main element I found to be lacking was the story; it was rather light. There are a few tense moments in the story, but overall, it seemed like the writers decided on a safer route. I was expecting somewhat darker and more philosophical themes to be used in the game. They are touched upon lightly, but not expanded to play any significant role. Given the premise, there's a whole world of deep possibilities that could be played out, but the writing just scratches the surface of this. In the end, I found myself wanting a little more out of the game.

All in all, the game was less than satisfactory for me and I'd give it a neutral rating, if I could. If you're new to the whole 'mass surveillance' idea and want to see a taste of what a game could do with that idea, then sure, go play this. But if you want something deeper, this isn't quite it.

Side note: I also bought and played the DLC and it's just more of the same, in my opinion.

I really want to recommend this game, but I can't. The marks of a quality product are there: An interesting surveillance state story, has great presentation and gameplay mechanics show great promise. The problem? Everything is mostly on rails and the little decision making the game allows you to make amounts to nothing. There's only 3 possible endings, all of them determined by endgame decisions that fail to represent the role that the player has had in the story. It feels forced, especially when you can clearly see potential targets talking trash about the goverment but can't do anything about it until much later, when your "superiors" (the devs) allow for it. The game as a whole is a great concept, but it needs more time in the oven.

Compelling psychological deduction game, piece together information found in newspapers, social media, personal data and prevent a terrorist attack, aka cyber stalking - the game.

The overall theme is not surprising given the title but the story takes some intriguing turns. The pacing worked great for me and the choices you make (the info you upload) have a lasting effect on the story, not just on whether you get "the one good or the one bad ending", so to speak.

You will not always know what the "correct" answer is and it is up to you to decide which often contradictory data chunks are relevant to the case. If you mindlessly upload everything without question and without considering the context, you will probably not have such a good time. 
I would have prefered if the develeopers didn't differetate between blue and yellow data chunks. They aren't that different anyway and I would recommend ignoring the color coding as much as you can.

I can also see this working great in an educational setting or for people who usually don't play video games.

I really enjoyed this game. The gameplay is very simple in that you search through a person's personal information that is stored online or in databases and basically drag and drop relevant bits of information (chunks of text) into a software that is used to determine if a person is a threat to the nation or not. Each bit of information can lead to access to more documents and I really enjoyed how that exploration helped flesh out the story universe. However only certain text chunks can be utilized and I often found some other information that might be more relevant to the story. 

It raises interesting questions about modern-day or even future surveillance, the fragmented parts of ourselves that we put out onto the internet, and how the things we put online, without context, can end up creating a narrative that might not be entirely true. If I were to rate this game, it would be a solid 8 out of 10.

This game honestly fucked me up a bit by the end of it.

At first it kinda comes off as a Death and Taxes kind of game, but no. It is one long single story arch that is honestly wonderfully crafted. My investment and intrigue in the game honestly just grew more and more as the game went on and went in turns I didn't expect. I often found myself expecting one culprit only to move on to another and another and another as I found and submitted more evidence.

I played the whole game in 5 hours, but honestly I will go back for more. I have more achievements to get and I want to see what else I can find. I still have a bunch of questions and I want to find the answers!

Game play wise the choice mechanics here are really interesting. Rather than just swipping information away like you do in most games like this, you are given loads of info and can pick and chose information that you submit based on what the system deems relevant for you to possibly submit. Then there are some bits of info that are game changing. You also can't go back and take back previously submitted information, previous info you have supplied can only be updated.

All the info is presented to you in a way that you can just select the highlighted sentences and submit the info. You can submit evidence without actually reading the whole articles or chats or what ever it is that highlighted sentence is in. However, that is because the system only selects what it finds relevant. Sometimes the context surrounding that sentence can drastically change it's implications. Which is an amazing way of proving one of many points in this game. If you look at the small picture and just submit the evidence based on what the system shows you, you will get a lot more things wrong. I know because at first I didn't read statements completely. Then I realized a few times I messed up, I wished I could take something back but I couldn't and slowly I became more cautious of what I submitted. This also applied to times that I submitted fishy or questionable evidence only to realize a few web pages or convos later that the info was inaccurate.

If you like thought provoking story lines. The kind of game that afterwards you question of you did the right things, this is a great game for you. It's slightly slow pacing at first, but if you can get passed that the game will have you hooked. Another good comparison would be that if you are into Black Mirrors on Netflix, this is a game you are sure to enjoy.

Everything Edward Snowden Warned Us About: The Game. There are two dimensions about Orwell's political commentary that are particularly powerful. One, that in this age of mass surveillance, drone warfare, informatics, etc., surveillance produces certain forms of intimacy. When the people you learn to profile and study can be led to arrest or even death, it's devastating; it demonstrates how surveillance demolishes those on both sides of the snooping relationship. Second, Orwell has done a phenomenal job in its lore and worldbuilding--websites have the character, look, and rhetoric of the kind of online media ecology that we see in the real internet. The quotidian dimension of this setting demonstrates how this mass surveillance of the control society has become so regularized and normalized within a historical moment most of us consider "normal" and safe. Orwell denaturalizes this to great effect.

All of that said, Orwell ends far too abruptly, with a climax that doesn't quite feel earned. This game could've easily gone on for twice as long, and the payoff probably would have been more rewarding. Nevertheless the accomplishments of the game put it squarely in the "positive" category for me. Quite an achievement.

This is a very interesting game, especially for anyone who has an interest in the surveillance state and the pros and cons of such a thing, mixed in with choices that really seem to matter.  I will admit that I have have, at the time of writing this review only played one playthrough, but the story was compelling and the information that I chose to put in/leave out really seemed to impact what was happening.  On top of that, the story is compelling, interesting and told through a very interesting way, feeding you snippets as you dig through the personal lives and media presence of several NPCs with various connections to one another, with a simple lock-off system that makes sense in-universe (we don't have clearance to investigate this person who has some connection to a potential suspect).

Beyond that, the only real issue I have with the game is the few interface bugs.  As the game went on, I found myself getting glitched to certain websites, mostly the [spoiler]work profile of the concerned one woman after she died in a shootout with law enforcement, and occasionally it would glitch to her dating profile.  This would normally happen when I was in either the listener or insider tools, seemingly never when I was on the reader tool already.  It would just switch me over as I tried to open a file on the insider, or load up into a machine, or even when I'd try opening a new conversation in the listener.[/spoiler]
One more slight drawback about the game is that sometimes you get told a bit too much by the game.  Game not letting you progress?  Something you thought was a lie was probably true.  Yellow highlight instead of blue?  You're going to get some information that conflicts with that.  I realise it would be a lot more work but a way to mark information as lies rather than just disabling it might help.  People don't always tell the truth and if you come to the conclusion that something true is a lie, it would be nice if the game didn't give away that you're wrong by just stopping time for you.  As for the other issue, it might be nice getting a window saying "Hey, this piece of information you're trying to add conflicts with this other information you've already added...which one do you think is true?", instead of just "Hey, at some point probably in the next 10 minutes you'll get another piece of information that will conflict with this here, we know that even though in-universe we haven't made the connection that that page with the conflicting information even exists!"

All in all a really great game with a simple premise, easy to learn with some fairly minor flaws that can honestly be overlooked most of the time.

Other than some slight annoyances in the mechanics: delay when uploading files, max type speed or speed speed not fast enough for skipping through 2nd playthrough, uploading onto wrong profile or an unsuccessful upload has the same color so therefore looks exactly like the successful upload, and some confusing prompts/options at times. Orwell tells a compelling story from a interesting perspective.

Every once in a while, a game will come along that you simply won’t put down and will try to finish in one sitting. For me, Orwell fits that category, for it was thoroughly engrossing.

As the name suggests, Orwell deals with privacy and government surveillance. You are an ‘investigator’ of the new Orwell application, an app which, with the right authorisation, allows you to snoop on people’s phone calls, e-mails and all their online histories at will.

It is a disturbing look into a surveillance state, and yet, by putting you in charge it opens the door (and your mind) to justifying the system.

In the introduction, there is a terrorist bombing that kills some people. That’s where you come in, you’re in to investigate the prime suspect and ultimately to bring down the terror cell. You pick datachunks, which is vital (and non-vital/misleading) information and assign it to a person of interest in order to shape a narrative about them.

For example, you can use it properly in order to keep the authorities informed about a person’s whereabouts or connections with other people. Likewise, you can misuse it, say you might see a Twitter conversation where someone says “oh that’s torture!” (in reference to being taken out nightclubbing to dance) and the system will update to suggest that the person in question is, actually, a genuine torturer.

It is pretty obvious that Orwell intends for you to use your best judgement in the situation, take it seriously as a proper investigative tool and suddenly the arguments for invasive surveillance look quite appealing, especially if you succeed in foiling terror actions. Use it inappropriately on the other hand and suddenly things look a bit bleak.

For me, Orwell’s story was enticing and gripping. I was captivated trying to deny the terror actions, but also by the investigation into the terror cell. I don’t want to spoil anything, but basically, I swept through this in one sitting, without breaks, in just over four hours.

Why not a higher score? Well, I did encounter some bugs. At one point in a new chapter it would keep defaulting back to the previous chapter’s screens. I had to reboot the game in order to cut this nonsense out and continue. Without these, I may very well have given a 9, but I think that perhaps, would be too generous given the nature of the game. Still, this is a very good game.

I really want this game to be good. The idea of being Big Brother fighting against freedom groups while they make comments about your injustice is fascinating. However, the game barely passes as a game and more of a click and listen to your boss speak. Only a few pieces of information are "conflicting," and once you decide on what conflicting data is correct, you can't undo your choice. Why would I not be able to update a database with new information? There are actually pieces of data that will replace older ones, so the mechanic is literally staring you in the face. Also, almost every piece of data you acquire results in your boss making some comment. A few are useful, such as him making an interesting connection. But have of them are "that's weird, huh." Or extremely stupid ones like "trouble in paradise, eh." The core game play loop is click on tab with red star, find blue highlights, drag them to the left, listen to boss be an idiot, repeat. If the game was left with the ability to select what text you believe is appropriate and then sent you on your own, it'd be much better. If you could assemble the reports and see the result, e.g., if a jury deemed your target guilty, then it'd be amazing. As it stands, its an amazing concept with terrible execution.

While this game has been my first foray into what I'd consider to be the "mystery" genre, I can tell its very unique from anything else I've played or I suspect is out there. Orwell isn't a who-done-it like anything else I've ever seen. There's no pipe smoking detective here drawing conclusions - just you, a surveillance state, their incredibly troubling spy software, a very well fleshed out world, and an imminent terrorist threat. 
The game asks you to not only solve the mystery but to draw your own conclusions on one very important moral question: do the ends always justify the means when it comes to keeping people safe? Your choice on this and other important pieces throughout the game change the outcome, inviting you to come back time and time again to see how it all could have been.
My only complaint: I NEED MORE! Orwell took me about 5 hours to complete, and the Ignorance is Strength DLC took me about 2 or 3 hours. Can we expect to see more content from Orwell? I don't know, but goddamn I sure hope so!

Interesting little game. To describe it best I might as well lead you through my experience as I played through it. 

After the start and a bit further in I started worrying whether it could really give one that special something that we are all looking for in games. Is it to linear? Do I really need to investigate? Is it a no-brainer drag and drop? Do my decisions even matter in the end? And certainly it took a bit but as the story opened up I caught myself questioning my previous thoughts and decisions more often. Was it a coincidence? Is it the truth or an attempt to mislead? What am I missing? This struggle continued for a while, clicking and reading through pages of information, until the story picked up the pace and gave me the opening for the final push. The positive jump in mood and anticipation of finally unraveling it all made the last stretch a very entertaining experience. One might ask: Is it just the ending then that is good? No, everything together, the conclusion just as much as the road leading up to it made it all worth it.

It wasn't perfect. I had some rare situations where I felt forced to make a questionable decision just to progress. And personally I might have wanted to see more irrelevant pieces of information that are better hidden and more indistinguishable from important ones. Maybe even a complete overhaul of the presentation of parse-able information which would make it harder to find them. Could have been a harder difficulty option? 

With that said. I can only recommend it. Give it a try.
